text: Once you can branch and loop, the next step is packaging that logic so you can reuse it instead of retyping it every time. JavaScript gives you three different ways to write a function, and they're not all equivalent.

A function declaration names the function up front with the word function. Here, getPriorityLabel takes a parameter called priority and returns a label based on it. Calling it with 1 returns Critical. One quirk worth knowing: function declarations are hoisted, meaning JavaScript makes them callable even from code written above the declaration itself, as long as it's in the same scope.

A function expression instead assigns an unnamed function to a variable - here, getLabel. Unlike a declaration, it is not hoisted: the variable exists early, but doesn't hold a working function until that line actually runs. Arrow functions are a shorter syntax for the same idea - this one-line version, double, skips the braces and the word return entirely, implicitly returning the result of the expression.

So you have three shapes to choose from. A declaration, hoisted and named with the function keyword. An expression, assigned to a variable, not hoisted. And an arrow function, the shortest syntax, which behaves differently in one important way covered next.

Regular functions and arrow functions handle the keyword this very differently. A regular function gets its own this, determined by how it's called - inside this ticket object's logRegular method, this correctly refers to the ticket. But logArrow, written as an arrow function, has no this of its own - it simply borrows whatever this was already in scope when it was defined, which is not the ticket object. This distinction comes back in much more depth in Chapter 2's lesson on scope.

Three function shapes, and one real behavioral difference in how this works that isn't just stylistic. Next up: arrays - lists of data, and the methods that let you search, transform, and filter them.
